ctx.x: I guess you've noticed the stop time in both records. This record was played probably 10 years or 12 years before Armstrong's record was played. I'll let you know how far the colored man has come.

Playing a tiger rag. This is Dixonland Jubilee by Kit Ory. This is only about a year old. Between this and the one that I'll play that was played almost 42 years ago, 41 years ago, you'll see the difference. That's what these white men call good music. Some of these tribes should go back in Africa and live over there and find out about the Negro place over there. This man is coming Louis Armstrong. That's Armstrong. items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: And Handy was given out about jazz.

ctx.x: Fletcher Henderson and Benny Morton of Kansas City were also among the first swing artists. Benny Morton's name is spelled M-O-R-T-O-N. Do you want me to read the letter to the editor? Just a moment.

These Negroes showed their appreciation after I had made it easy for them to come up and open his publishing concern. He didn't know me. That 20 years had passed. In 1936, Lou Gensler had a big broadcast. He tried to locate us to put us in the beginning and Benny Goodman as the end. In other words, the beginning and end. items.q: i played saint louis blues for handy

ctx.x: it's quite a popular belief i believe that the original dixieland jazz band and you in particular discriminated against the colored people if that is so perhaps some of these people who think themselves so clever and these people who have all the say so in the books and magazines and so on would care to reflect on the number of tunes recorded and played by the original dixieland jazz band that were written by colored men that doesn't look like the discrimination to me think of them there's mammy oh mine by maceo…

discrimination to me and not only that i played saint louis blues for handy oh yes of course i was forgetting that and our picture was on all these colored publications it was royal garden blues for spencer and clarence that's right spencer claren williams our pictures was on all their publications they were willing to ride our back to get up now that they got up there they tried to bury me but there's two lane archers opened up and i hope to see the future historians and scholars look into the truth and see…

thing before i close that there are recordings made at the same time as yours around 1921 by colored people of numbers like royal garden blues and jasmine blues and i listened to them and they do not contain anything like the same spirit of jazz as yours do they're obviously they're stodgy they're obviously striving after it they're the first attempts to follow and they're trying very hard perhaps they're trying too hard but they don't get there they don't flow they don't move they don't excite the dance anyone…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: I said, let me go and see him. I may be able to record it for him.

ctx.x: By blowing the cornet, I was making this. Da, And by forcing, the back part would go. You understand what I mean? I see. And that gave me an idea of putting that into the throat. And I tried to make that on the horn, and I made it on the horn. On the horn. See, on this cornet. Not this one. The one that I had was a little bit. A piece of junk. Now, that's the whole tiger rag in completion. It has a little part of the quadrill. And if anyone says they have it in there, you play the tiger, if you played the tiger…

He wouldn't even play jazz or the blues. He'd committed to paper. This Negro here had went into the hands of the receiver. And I know this tune by the name of Jobo Blues. And I used to play it in the band. And Russell Roberts says to me, you know whose tune that is? I said, no. He says, that's Hannity's tune. I says, it's a damn good tune. I said, let me go and see him. I may be able to record it for him. At that time, he was in the hands of the receiver. I went on over there. And he wasn't there. I spoke to his…
